angle: follow one account and then one request: the account joins a tree (organization, root, OUs), the management account pays one bill for every account, a request in a member account passes the SCP of every level, SCPs stop at the management account and at outside principals (RCPs and declarative policies cover the rest), Control Tower builds and governs the tree, and AWS RAM lets the accounts use one resource instead of copies
base: Pattern: _build/style/exemplar/ (README: ten things to imitate, ten common mistakes), _build/work/10-vpc/brief.json for the brief shape. Chapter 03 (IAM) teaches the policy evaluation logic, including how SCPs and RCPs limit permissions (03 brief section 'aws-allows-a-request-only-when-nothing-denies-and-something-allows'); this chapter owns Organizations itself and cross-references 03 for the evaluation logic with an xref marker. Do not re-teach permissions boundaries, session policies or the full evaluation order here.

Time-box guidance: 870/120 + 7 prompts = about 15 minutes, the medium target 12 plus the 3-minute tolerance. Do not add a Look first section and do not add a second compare table: either one pushes the file over the reading budget.

sections.heading: Predict
sections.plan: Two prompts, each ending with '?'. Predict 1 is the gist trap (<!-- gist-trap -->): 'A company attaches an SCP to the organization root that denies deleting log buckets. Can an administrator in the management account still delete a log bucket?' (common sense says no, because the root covers everything; the truth is yes). Predict 2: 'In AWS Control Tower, does a detective control stop a developer who tries to make a bucket public?' Spell out SCP in the prompt (service control policy). Answers appear only in Check (U4). At most 80 words.

sections.heading: In one breath
sections.plan: Say it (one-breath definition, at most 25 words, for example: 'AWS Organizations puts your accounts in one tree. Policies on a branch limit every account below it, and one account pays the bill.' with a fact link where a hard fact appears). Then '**The problem it solves.**' in one sentence (one account holds everything, so one mistake reaches everything). Then 'Predict the picture: which accounts does an SCP on the Workloads OU reach?' with the hero organizations-hero inside a reveal, its caption and its 4 numbered steps (text fixed in diagrams below). Then the Startup example callout with the Problem of data/startup.json chapter 04 word for word (42 words plus the label). Keep the hero alt at about 30 words. At most 200 words in all.

sections.heading: Words that go together
sections.plan: A words table of 5 rows (see words_table). Cell 1 is the term field of data/terms.json. Four of the five terms are term_requests: the orchestrator adds them to the bank before the writers start; until then use <!-- needs-term: <term> --> at the first use. At most 110 words.

sections.heading: Choose it or not
sections.plan: One compare table, 'AWS Organizations alone or AWS Control Tower' (see compare_tables), three columns, four rows, then its bold **Deciding question:** line. At most 160 words. The SCP, RCP and declarative policy comparison is the table of How it works subsection 4, not a second table here.

sections.heading: Signals and traps
sections.plan: A signals table of 6 rows (see signals; headers exactly 'The stem says | Think | Because | But not if'), then the fixed H3 'Traps' with the 3 fast traps, each one list item 'Wrong belief ... Truth ...' that ends with <!-- trap: <id> --> (see traps with placed_in 1-fast.md#signals-and-traps). At most 260 words; keep each row near 25 words.

sections.heading: Changed recently
sections.plan: Two examinable entries (see changed_recently.fast) in the D6 form, at most 130 words in all. Pending fr-0031 (display '5' on organizations-scp-max-attached-per-entity for the Old line): until it is filled, write the Old value without a link and add <!-- needs-display: organizations-scp-max-attached-per-entity "5" -->.

sections.heading: Check
sections.plan: Two Check prompts parallel to Predict, each answered in its reveal, with a separate '**Predict <n>:**' paragraph (U4). Check 1: 'An SCP on the root denies s3:DeleteBucket. Does it stop the root user of a member account?' (Yes: [including the member account's root user](iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user).) Predict 1: No, SCPs do not restrict users or roles in the management account. Check 2: 'A detective control reports a public bucket in an enrolled account. Is the bucket still public until someone changes it?' (Yes: a detective control [provides alerts through the dashboard](control-tower-detective-alerts-dashboard-status); a preventive control blocks the action.) Predict 2: No, a detective control does not stop the developer. At most 90 words.

sections.heading: Recap from memory
sections.plan: Three Recap prompts with reveals, each asking only for a sentence, row or cell that 1-fast.md states above (U4): 1. Which account do SCPs not restrict? (hero step 4 or the first trap). 2. What is the deciding question of 'AWS Organizations alone or AWS Control Tower'? 3. Which service shares the subnets of one VPC with other accounts in the organization? (signals row 6). At most 100 words.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.minutes: sum of the subsection time boxes (4 + 3 + 5 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 24)
sections.intro: One line of at most 25 words before the first H3 that spells out the short forms used below: organizational unit (OU), service control policy (SCP), resource control policy (RCP), AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). End it with <!-- xref: 03 IAM policy evaluation logic for SCPs and RCPs -->.
sections.order_note: Teaching order follows one account and then one request: the account joins a tree (1), the management account pays for every account in the tree (2), a request in a member account must pass the SCP of every level (3), two kinds of principal stand outside the SCPs and need other tools (4), Control Tower builds the tree and puts controls on its OUs (5), and the accounts use one shared resource instead of copies (6).

sections.heading: An organization is a tree of accounts with one root and one management account

plan.problem: A team keeps development, testing and production in one AWS account. One wrong permission or one stolen key then reaches all three, because the account is the boundary.
trace: **Group the accounts.** An organization is [a collection of AWS accounts] in a [hierarchical, tree-like structure] with [a root at the top] (organizations-organization-is-tree-of-accounts); an organization has [1] root (organizations-one-root-per-organization).

**Nest OUs.** An OU is [a group of AWS accounts within an organization], and [An OU can also contain other OUs] (organizations-ou-is-group-of-accounts), at most [Five levels of OUs deep] (organizations-ou-max-nesting-five-levels). An account is a [member of only one OU at a time] (organizations-faq-account-one-ou-at-a-time).

**Add accounts.** Creating and inviting accounts [can be done only from the management account] (organizations-create-invite-only-from-management-account). An invited account [must accept or reject the request] (organizations-faq-invited-account-must-accept) within [15 days] (organizations-invitation-expires-15-days).

**Turn on the policies.** All features is [the default feature set] (organizations-all-features-is-default-feature-set); organization policies need it: [when all features are enabled] (organizations-policies-need-all-features).
plan.table: How an account joins (compare kind, columns: Question | Created in the organization | Invited). Rows: role for the management account: [automatically creates an IAM role] named [OrganizationAccountAccessRole] (organizations-created-account-gets-access-role) | the administrator can [choose to create an IAM role] (organizations-invited-account-access-role-optional); acceptance: none needed | accepts within [15 days] (organizations-invitation-expires-15-days); removal: [at least four days] after creation (organizations-remove-created-account-wait-four-days) | no waiting period (same fact: [Invited accounts aren't subject to this waiting period]).
plan.why: Why accounts and not tags? AWS treats an account as one of the [security, access, and billing boundaries] (organizations-account-is-security-access-billing-boundary). If something goes wrong in one account, [the impacts can be contained] (organizations-account-isolation-limits-blast-radius). Tags inside one account give no such boundary.
plan.exam_signal: 'isolate production from development' points to separate accounts in one organization, because separate accounts separate, [by default, the resources and data] of each environment (organizations-separate-accounts-prod-nonprod-by-default).
plan.body_extras: One sentence: [You cannot change which account] [is the management account] (organizations-management-account-cannot-be-changed). Optional half sentence: a member account belongs to [only one organization at a time] (organizations-member-account-one-organization-at-a-time).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: accounts sit in OUs under one root. The thing to watch is that an invited account gets no access role.
plan.stop_and_answer: The prod account sits in the Workloads OU. The security team also wants it in the Security OU, so that the policies of both OUs apply. Can the team do that? Answer: No; an account is a [member of only one OU at a time] (organizations-faq-account-one-ou-at-a-time). Attach the policy to a parent OU instead: nested OUs [inherit the policies from the parent OU] (organizations-nested-ous-inherit-parent-policies).

sections.heading: The management account pays one bill that combines the usage of every account

plan.problem: Twelve accounts that each pay their own bill each reach the price tiers alone, and a discount that one account bought helps only that account.
trace: **One payer.** The management account has [the role of a payer account] and is [responsible for paying all charges] (organizations-management-account-pays-all-charges).

**Combined tiers.** AWS treats the accounts [as if they were one account]: [AWS combines the usage from all accounts] to choose the volume pricing tier (organizations-billing-treats-accounts-as-one-for-tiers). AWS also [applies the free tier to the total usage] (organizations-free-tier-applies-to-total-org-usage).

**Shared commitments.** Consolidated billing [shares the volume pricing discounts, Reserved Instance discounts] and Savings Plans (organizations-consolidated-billing-combined-usage-shares-discounts). [Commitments benefit the account owner first], then the [remaining benefits can be shared] (organizations-ri-sp-benefit-owner-account-first).

**Reports by team.** Members [can still see their usage and charges], but [They can't view or obtain data] of other accounts (organizations-billing-management-account-charged-monthly). [Only the management account in an organization] can activate tags in the [cost allocation tags manager] (organizations-cost-allocation-tags-management-account).
plan.table: Optional two-column table 'Billing item | In an organization' (compare kind): volume pricing tiers | [AWS combines the usage from all accounts]; free tier | [applies the free tier to the total usage]; Reserved Instances and Savings Plans | [Commitments benefit the account owner first]; AWS credits | shared [by default (Credit sharing turned on)] (organizations-credit-sharing-on-by-default). Leave the table out if the subsection goes over 230 words all-in.
plan.why: Why one bill? An account is [default means by which AWS costs are allocated] (organizations-account-default-cost-allocation), so separate accounts already split the costs, and one payer lets AWS price the usage of the whole organization together.
plan.exam_signal: 'one bill and volume discounts across all accounts' points to consolidated billing in AWS Organizations, [offered at no additional cost] (organizations-consolidated-billing-combined-usage-shares-discounts).
plan.body_extras: The management account can [Activate or deactivate sharing for individual accounts] (organizations-management-account-controls-ri-sp-sharing). Do not write that the bill shows the OU structure, and do not link organizations-faq-bill-does-not-reflect-ou-structure here (its volatility is not stable). <!-- xref: 41 cost allocation tags and Savings Plans -->
plan.say_it: The short answer is: the management account pays one combined bill. The thing to watch is that member accounts see only their own charges.
plan.stop_and_answer: In one organization, account A bought a Reserved Instance that it uses only half of the time. Account B runs matching usage. Can account B get the discount? Answer: Yes, unless sharing is turned off: [Commitments benefit the account owner first], and the [remaining benefits can be shared] (organizations-ri-sp-benefit-owner-account-first); the management account can turn sharing off for one account (organizations-management-account-controls-ri-sp-sharing).

sections.heading: An action is allowed only if an SCP at every level allows it

plan.problem: A security team wants one rule that every member account obeys, including the administrators of each account.
trace: **Start from FullAWSAccess.** Organizations attaches [FullAWSAccess] [to every root, OU and account], and [This policy allows all services and actions] (organizations-fullawsaccess-attached-by-default).

**Walk down the path.** For an action to be allowed, [there must be an explicit Allow statement] [at every level from the root] through each OU to the account itself (organizations-scp-allow-needed-at-every-level). A level without an allow denies: SCPs use [a deny-by-default model] (organizations-scp-deny-by-default-model).
**A deny wins below it.** A Deny at one level applies to [all the OUs and member accounts underneath it] (organizations-scp-deny-at-any-level-applies-below).

**IAM must still allow.** [An SCP never grants permissions] (iam-scp-never-grants-permissions); the result is [the intersection between those allowed by the SCP and the permissions granted to the principal by IAM permission policies] (iam-scp-faq-effective-permissions-intersection). <!-- xref: 03 IAM policy evaluation logic -->
plan.table: Truth table (compare kind, 5 columns: Case | Root | Workloads OU | prod account | Result). Row 1: FullAWSAccess | FullAWSAccess | FullAWSAccess | Allowed if IAM allows. Row 2: FullAWSAccess | FullAWSAccess plus Deny on ec2:TerminateInstances | FullAWSAccess | Denied, also for an administrator. Row 3: FullAWSAccess | allows only EC2 and S3 | FullAWSAccess plus Allow for Lambda | Lambda: denied, because the OU level does not allow it. Link the result cells (organizations-scp-allow-needed-at-every-level, organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override); cells at most 15 words.
plan.why: Why every level? Each level is a filter that its owner controls. If an account could add back what its OU removed, the OU's guardrail would not hold for that account.
plan.exam_signal: 'no one in the member accounts, including administrators, can' points to an SCP with a Deny on the root or on the OU, because users [can't use that permission] even when the administrator [attaches the AdministratorAccess IAM policy] (organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override).
plan.body_extras: Member principals [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account] (iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps). Optional half sentence: AWS recommends an SCP at the root that denies [organizations:LeaveOrganization and account:CloseAccount] (organizations-scp-deny-leave-and-close-recommended).
plan.spot_the_bug: Prompt: 'To protect the audit trail in the prod account, a security team attaches an SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging to the Security OU. The prod account is in the Workloads OU. A prod administrator can still stop logging. Where is the bug?' Reveal: the Deny applies only to [all the OUs and member accounts underneath it] (organizations-scp-deny-at-any-level-applies-below); the prod account is not under the Security OU. Attach the SCP to the root or to the Workloads OU. Before any root attachment, AWS strongly recommends testing in an OU: [don't attach SCPs to the root] without testing (organizations-scp-test-in-ou-not-root).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a deny anywhere above the account wins. The thing to watch is that every level must also allow the action.
plan.stop_and_answer: The root and the Workloads OU keep FullAWSAccess. The Workloads OU also has an SCP that denies ec2:TerminateInstances. The prod account is in a child OU of Workloads. An administrator in prod has AdministratorAccess. Can the administrator terminate an instance? Answer: No; the Deny applies to [all the OUs and member accounts underneath it] (organizations-scp-deny-at-any-level-applies-below), and users [can't use that permission] even with AdministratorAccess (organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override).

sections.heading: SCPs do not limit the management account or principals outside the organization

plan.problem: The SCPs now guard every member account. Two kinds of principal stand outside them, and both can still change or read data.
trace: **The management account.** SCPs [affect only member accounts]; they do not restrict [users or roles in the management account] (organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account). So [keep them out of the management account]: workloads and resources (organizations-keep-resources-out-of-management-account).
**The member root user is inside.** An SCP restricts the member account's principals, [including the member account's root user] (iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user).

**Outside principals.** SCPs [do not affect users or roles from accounts outside the organization] (iam-scp-not-outside-principals-or-resource-policies). An RCP does: RCPs can affect [principals external to your organization] (organizations-rcp-affects-external-principals-scp-only-internal).

**Security tools in a member account.** A delegated administrator account gets [some administrative permissions for that service] and helps [reduce the usage of the management account] (organizations-delegated-admin-for-service-permissions); SCPs still apply to it (organizations-scp-applies-to-delegated-admin-accounts). <!-- xref: 09 detection services with a delegated administrator -->
plan.table: Compare table (4 columns: Question | SCP | RCP | Declarative policy). Rows: What it limits | principals of member accounts ([SCPs are principal-centric controls]) | resources of member accounts ([RCPs are resource-centric controls]) (both organizations-scp-principal-centric-rcp-resource-centric) | the configuration of a service ([centrally configure and manage AWS services], organizations-policy-categories-authorization-declarative). Reaches principals outside the organization | no | yes (organizations-rcp-affects-external-principals-scp-only-internal) | not applicable. Applies in the management account | no (organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account) | no (iam-rcp-no-effect-on-management-account) | yes, when attached to the root ([including the management account for the organization], organizations-declarative-policy-at-root-includes-management). Where it is enforced | API authorization | API authorization ([authorization policies regulate access to APIs]) | [enforced in the service's control plane] (organizations-declarative-policy-control-plane-not-api).
plan.why: Why can an SCP not stop an outside principal? [SCPs are principal-centric controls] (organizations-scp-principal-centric-rcp-resource-centric): they limit the principals of your member accounts, and another company's role is not one of them. A resource-side control is needed for that.
plan.exam_signal: 'principals outside the organization must not access the company's buckets, even if a bucket policy allows them' points to an RCP, because a blocked permission holds even when the owner attaches a policy that [allows full access to any user] (organizations-rcp-resource-policy-cannot-override).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: RCPs, declarative policies and the data perimeter (at most 150 words). Custom RCPs use Deny: [The effect of Allow is only supported] in RCPFullAWSAccess (organizations-rcp-allow-only-in-rcpfullawsaccess). [RCPs do not apply to AWS managed keys] in AWS KMS (organizations-rcp-not-aws-managed-kms-keys). An RCP [don't affect resources from accounts outside the organization] (organizations-rcp-applies-to-own-resources-even-external-callers). Declarative policies can [block public internet access to Amazon VPC resources] (organizations-declarative-policy-blocks-vpc-public-access), show [customizable error messages] (organizations-faq-declarative-customizable-error-messages), and [the configuration is always maintained] when the service adds features (organizations-declarative-policy-maintained-for-new-features). SCPs and RCPs together build a [data perimeter around your identities and your resources] (organizations-scp-rcp-independent-data-perimeter): the resource side is [applied on identities with an SCP] (iam-data-perimeter-resource-scp-resourceorgid), the identity side is [applied on resources with an RCP] (iam-data-perimeter-identity-rcp-principalorgid).
plan.body_extras: No Exam signal on service-linked roles here: they are a Go deeper detail of chapter 03. Do not write that RCPs cover every AWS service (iam-rcp-subset-of-services is chapter 03's).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: SCPs limit the principals of your member accounts. The thing to watch is the management account, which SCPs do not limit.
plan.stop_and_answer: An SCP on the root denies s3:GetObject on a company bucket for every principal. A partner's role in another company's AWS account is allowed s3:GetObject by the bucket policy, and the partner's own IAM policy allows it too. Can the partner's role read objects? Answer: Yes; SCPs [do not affect users or roles from accounts outside the organization] (iam-scp-not-outside-principals-or-resource-policies). An RCP on the root, or a change to the bucket policy, would stop it (organizations-rcp-affects-external-principals-scp-only-internal).

sections.heading: A Control Tower landing zone applies preventive and detective controls to registered OUs

plan.problem: Seven accounts built by hand drift apart, and each new account starts without the rules of the others.
trace: **Build the landing zone.** A landing zone is [a well-architected, multi-account environment] (control-tower-landing-zone-definition). Control Tower [orchestrates the capabilities of several other AWS services] [to build a landing zone] (control-tower-sets-up-governs-multi-account) on top of Organizations, with [preventive guardrails using SCPs and RCPs] (control-tower-faq-built-on-organizations-scps-rcps).

**Create the shared accounts.** Setup creates [the Security OU and the optional Sandbox OU] (control-tower-landing-zone-setup-actions) and the shared accounts: the management account, [the log archive account, and the audit account] (control-tower-shared-accounts). [All actions are logged], including [actions from the AWS Control Tower management account] (control-tower-logs-all-actions-including-management).
**Vend new accounts.** Account Factory is [a configurable account template] that [automates the process of applying controls and policies] (control-tower-account-factory-template).

**Put controls on an OU.** A control [applies to an entire organizational unit (OU)] (control-tower-control-applies-to-whole-ou). [Preventive controls prevent actions from occurring]; [Detective controls detect specific events when they occur]; proactive controls check resources [before the resources are provisioned] (control-tower-preventive-detective-proactive-defined).
plan.table: Truth table (compare kind, columns: Control type | Built with | What happens to a noncompliant action). Preventive | SCPs, [Resource Control Policies (RCPs), and declarative policies] | the action is blocked. Detective | [detective controls are implemented using AWS Config rules] | it happens, and the control [provides alerts through the dashboard] (control-tower-detective-alerts-dashboard-status). Proactive | [implemented using AWS CloudFormation hooks] (all three: control-tower-control-types-mechanisms) | blocked only for resources created [by means of CloudFormation stack operations] (control-tower-proactive-only-cloudformation).
plan.why: Why keep detective controls that do not block? A preventive control stops the actions you can name in advance; a detective control reports the resources that already break a rule. AWS says to use Control Tower [preventive controls in combination with] the detective controls of Security Hub CSPM (control-tower-faq-complementary-to-security-hub). <!-- xref: 09 Security Hub CSPM -->
plan.exam_signal: 'new accounts must get the same controls automatically, with the LEAST operational overhead' points to Control Tower with Account Factory, which builds [a secure, compliant, multi-account AWS environment] (control-tower-easiest-way-secure-multi-account) and [automates the process of applying controls and policies] (control-tower-account-factory-template). Do not link the display 'the easiest way to set up and govern': 'set up' is a banned word (STYLE 3), and a link text is prose.
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: enrollment, guidance levels and the Region deny control (at most 150 words; in this order of priority, stop when the words run out). In a registered OU, preventive controls reach accounts [under the OU, enrolled and unenrolled], but [detective controls apply to enrolled accounts only] (control-tower-preventive-apply-unenrolled-detective-enrolled-only). An existing account [must have the AWSControlTowerExecution role enabled] and [must not have existing AWS Config resources] to enroll (control-tower-enroll-needs-execution-role-no-config). Guidance is mandatory, strongly recommended or elective (control-tower-guidance-levels); [By default, Strongly recommended controls are not enabled] (control-tower-strongly-recommended-elective-off-by-default), and from [Landing Zone version 4.0] [mandatory controls are no longer applied by default] (control-tower-lz4-mandatory-not-default). The Region deny control: [You cannot deny access to your home Region], and global services [such as IAM and AWS Organizations, are exempt] (control-tower-region-deny-exemptions). Preventive controls are [not applied to the management account] (control-tower-preventive-not-on-management-account). A control was formerly called a guardrail (control-tower-guardrail-renamed-control; no date exists, write none).
plan.body_extras: The audit log: an organization trail logs every account; [Member accounts can see the organization trail] but [can't modify or delete it] (organizations-org-trail-members-cannot-modify-or-delete), and you need [the management account or a delegated administrator account] [to create an organization trail] (organizations-org-trail-only-from-management-account). Mandatory controls on the Security OU [prevents changes to bucket policy] and [prevents deletion of Amazon S3 buckets] [in the log archive account] (control-tower-mandatory-log-archive-bucket-controls). Do NOT write that Control Tower creates the organization trail or turns it on: that fact (control-tower-organization-level-trail) was rejected and no verified fact replaces it (brief.v0 d063). <!-- xref: 37 CloudTrail organization trail -->
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Control Tower builds the accounts and puts controls on each OU. The thing to watch is accounts created outside it.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team turns on a proactive control that requires encryption on new S3 buckets. A developer then creates an unencrypted bucket with the AWS CLI, not with CloudFormation. Does the control stop the bucket? Answer: Not necessarily; proactive controls check resources created [by means of CloudFormation stack operations] and [may not affect requests that are made directly] (control-tower-proactive-only-cloudformation). A preventive control, or a detective control that reports the bucket, covers that path.

sections.heading: AWS RAM shares one resource with other accounts instead of copying it

plan.problem: A network team builds one VPC and one set of DNS rules. Every other account needs them, and copies in each account would drift.
trace: **Create a resource share.** Add the resources, [choosing a managed permission] for each resource type, and name who gets access (ram-faq-resource-share-steps). RAM uses the permission to [generate a resource-based policy] for each resource (ram-managed-permission-generates-resource-policy).

**Choose the principals.** RAM shares with any account ([You can share resources with any AWS account.]) and with OUs or the whole organization when [sharing within your organization is enabled] (ram-faq-share-with-any-account-ous-if-enabled). Inside the organization [AWS RAM doesn't send invitations to principals] (ram-org-sharing-no-invitations); outside it, [The recipient must accept the invitation] (ram-outside-org-needs-invitation).
**Check the resource type.** [Some resource types can't be shared] outside the organization (ram-some-types-only-within-organization).

**Use it in its Region.** Most shared resources are Regional: [you must direct your operations to that Region] (ram-regional-resources-used-in-their-region). The consumer's own policies [also apply to the shared resource] (ram-consumer-account-policies-apply).

sections.heading: FAQ quick-fire
sections.plan: Five 'FAQ <n>.' prompts (see faq), each answered in one clause in its reveal and followed by an AWS quote block of whole sentences from the fact's evidence quote, with the FAQ page link. At most 250 words.

traps.belief: An SCP attached to the organization root limits every account, the management account too.
traps.truth: SCPs affect only member accounts; they do not restrict users or roles in the management account, so AWS says to keep resources out of it.

traps.belief: Tags and IAM policies inside one account isolate production as well as a separate account does.
traps.truth: An account is a security, access and billing boundary; separate accounts for production and non-production separate their resources and data by default.

traps.belief: A detective control in AWS Control Tower stops a noncompliant action.
traps.truth: Preventive controls prevent actions; detective controls detect events when they occur and alert through the dashboard.

traps.belief: An SCP that allows a service, attached directly to the account, is enough for the account to use that service.
traps.truth: An explicit Allow must exist at every level from the root through each OU to the account; an OU that does not allow the service blocks it for every account below.

traps.belief: An SCP on the root also stops users from other AWS accounts that a bucket policy lets in.
traps.truth: SCPs affect only principals inside the organization; an RCP can limit what principals outside the organization do with your resources.

traps.belief: After Control Tower is set up, its controls govern every account in the organization.
traps.truth: Accounts and OUs created outside Control Tower are not bound by its controls until you register the OU or enroll the account.

traps.belief: AWS RAM can share any resource type with any AWS account or principal.
traps.truth: Some resource types stay inside the organization: subnets and security groups can be shared only with accounts in the same organization, and subnets not with IAM roles or users.

trap_reuse_from_other_chapters.note: Distractors can also cite these chapter 03 trap ids (lint.traps() knows every brief): iam-trap-scp-grants (an SCP that allows a service gives access), iam-trap-admin-ignores-scp (AdministratorAccess or the root user can do everything in a member account), iam-trap-allow-beats-deny, iam-trap-boundary-limits-root. question_slots.note: An existing organization with all features; the administrators of the member accounts have AdministratorAccess. The company must ensure that no member account can leave the organization. Key: an SCP on the root that denies organizations:LeaveOrganization (organizations-scp-deny-leave-and-close-recommended, organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override). Distractors: an IAM policy with an explicit Deny attached to the administrator role in each member account (violates-qualifier and the administrators can detach it; misconception sentence); the same SCP attached to the management account only (wrong-configuration, trap organizations-trap-scp-on-management-account); a Control Tower detective control that reports the LeaveOrganization call (sibling-confusion, trap organizations-trap-detective-blocks). Do not mention the 2026-07-10 console default for new organizations.

Qualifier none. An SCP on the root denies logs:DeleteLogGroup. A role in the management account deletes a log group, and the call succeeds. Why? Key: SCPs do not restrict users or roles in the management account (organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account). Distractors: the role's AdministratorAccess policy overrides the SCP (trap iam-trap-admin-ignores-scp); an SCP inherited from the root does not apply until it is attached to each account directly (misconception; organizations-faq-policies-enforced-automatically-on-new-account); SCPs restrict IAM users but not IAM roles (misconception; iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user names users and roles). Options of difficulty 1 can be short (2 to 45 words).

Use a scenario different from the Spot the bug and the Stop and answer of the section. The Workloads OU replaced FullAWSAccess with an SCP that allows only Amazon EC2, Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudWatch. One account under Workloads must start to use Amazon Athena; every other account under Workloads must keep the allow list unchanged. The account already has FullAWSAccess and an SCP that allows athena:* attached directly, and calls still fail. Key: create a separate OU for that account whose path allows Athena at every level (for example under the root with FullAWSAccess plus the needed guardrails) and move the account there (organizations-scp-allow-needed-at-every-level, organizations-ou-policy-inherited-by-accounts). Distractors: attach one more SCP that allows athena:* to the account (wrong-configuration, trap organizations-trap-account-level-allow-enough); add athena:* to the IAM policy of the team's role (sibling-confusion, trap iam-trap-allow-beats-deny does not fit; give it the misconception 'an IAM allow can pass an SCP level that does not allow the action'); add athena:* to the allow list of the Workloads OU (violates-qualifier: it works for the account but breaks the requirement that the other Workloads accounts keep their allow list; this is the plausible second finalist of a difficulty 3 question).

A company runs development, testing and production in one account. It must isolate production, keep the audit logs in a separate account, and apply the same guardrails to every future account. Key: an AWS Control Tower landing zone with Account Factory for new accounts (control-tower-easiest-way-secure-multi-account, control-tower-shared-accounts, control-tower-account-factory-template). Distractors: tags, IAM policies and permissions boundaries in the one account (trap organizations-trap-tags-isolate-like-accounts); AWS Organizations with accounts created by hand and a baseline deployed with CloudFormation StackSets (violates-qualifier; organizations-stacksets-provision-to-accounts); one VPC for each environment in the one account (sibling-confusion; misconception 'a VPC is an isolation boundary for IAM permissions').

(Select TWO.) Twelve accounts each have their own bill. Finance wants one bill, prices based on the combined usage, and a monthly cost report for each team; every team tags its resources with a team tag. Keys: create an organization and invite the other accounts (organizations-billing-treats-accounts-as-one-for-tiers, organizations-management-account-pays-all-charges); activate the team tag as a cost allocation tag in the management account (organizations-cost-allocation-tags-management-account). Distractors: activate the cost allocation tag in each member account (impossible-feature, why links organizations-cost-allocation-tags-management-account); create a separate organization for each team (violates the one-bill requirement; misconception); attach an SCP to the root that allows the billing actions (keyword-bait, trap iam-trap-scp-grants). Do not use organizations-faq-bill-does-not-reflect-ou-structure (volatility not stable).

Qualifier none. An existing account joined the organization by invitation. An administrator in the management account cannot assume OrganizationAccountAccessRole in it. What is the reason? Key: Organizations creates that role only in accounts that it creates; for an invited account an administrator must create the role (organizations-created-account-gets-access-role, organizations-invited-account-access-role-optional). Distractors: an SCP on the root blocks the management account (trap organizations-trap-scp-on-management-account); the invitation expired after 15 days (misconception: the account already joined; organizations-invitation-expires-15-days); the account must first be moved into an OU (misconception).

question_slots.note: Strict twin: the stems differ in one phrase, the four option texts are identical, the key moves. Shared stem: a company with all features enabled stores data in Amazon S3 buckets in its member accounts. Changed phrase here: 'Principals in the company's accounts must not be able to access S3 buckets that belong to other AWS organizations.' Key: (A) an SCP on the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the resource belongs to the company's organization (organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access, iam-data-perimeter-resource-scp-resourceorgid). Identical options: (A) as above; (B) an RCP on the root that denies Amazon S3 access unless the principal belongs to the company's organization (here wrong: an RCP [don't affect resources from accounts outside the organization], organizations-rcp-applies-to-own-resources-even-external-callers; misconception 'an RCP limits what your own principals do with other companies' resources'); (C) a permissions boundary on every IAM role in every member account (violates-qualifier; misconception); (D) turn on trusted access for Amazon S3 in AWS Organizations (keyword-bait; organizations-trusted-access-service-acts-on-behalf; misconception). Write the options in neutral words that fit both stems.

A company has a Control Tower landing zone. Some teams create accounts with the AWS Organizations CreateAccount API in an OU that is not registered, and the controls do not apply there. Every future account must get the controls automatically. Key: register the OU with Control Tower and create new accounts with Account Factory (control-tower-accounts-outside-not-bound, control-tower-register-ous-enroll-accounts, control-tower-account-factory-template). Distractors: attach the Control Tower SCPs by hand to each new account (violates-qualifier; misconception); turn on more detective controls in the landing zone, which then cover every account of the organization (trap organizations-trap-control-tower-governs-all-accounts); deploy AWS Config rules to each account with CloudFormation StackSets (sibling-confusion; misconception that detection enforces). Do not make automatic enrollment the key or a deciding option: its facts are frequently changing.

An organization has 40 accounts and adds accounts every month. The network account owns Route 53 Resolver rules that every account must use, future accounts included. tasks.title: Share a subnet with AWS RAM and read the permission it uses
tasks.kills: "Sharing a resource with AWS RAM copies the resource into the other account."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, three resources, $0 (vpc-faq-no-charge-for-vpc-itself, ram-faq-no-additional-cost): create a VPC saa-organizations-t01 (10.0.0.0/16) tagged book=saa and task=organizations-t01; create one subnet, tagged; create a resource share saa-organizations-t01 that holds the subnet and no principal, tagged, with external principals not allowed. Read the share's resources and read the managed permission attached for the subnet type: every type has a default AWS managed permission (ram-faq-aws-managed-permission-default-per-type), which RAM uses to generate a resource-based policy (ram-managed-permission-generates-resource-policy). Observe that the subnet keeps its own ID and stays in its Region (ram-regional-resources-used-in-their-region): nothing was copied (ram-reduces-overhead-no-duplicate-resources). No break-it step (medium break_it_steps_min 0); do not add a principal: an account ID typed by mistake sends a real invitation. Cleanup in reverse order: delete the resource share, delete the subnet, delete the VPC. Verify: describe-vpcs filtered by tag task=organizations-t01 returns nothing, and get-resource-shares filtered by the tag returns nothing. Commands must come from the RAM and EC2 CLI reference pages in the corpus (tasks check-cli --reference). Writer check: if the CLI reference shows that create-resource-share for a subnet needs an organization with sharing enabled, park the task and report it; the read-only alternative is list-permissions for the resource type ec2:Subnet.

speak.prompt: How do I make sure that even a production administrator cannot turn off the audit log?
speak.note: Short answer: make the trail an organization trail from the management account; member accounts, their administrators included, can see it but cannot change or delete it. How it works: the trail logs every account into the log archive account, and Control Tower's mandatory controls stop changes to that account's log buckets; an SCP Deny in the member accounts also holds against AdministratorAccess. Watch: the management account is outside SCPs and preventive controls, so keep very few people there. In your case: 'Who can sign in to the management account today?' Must not say: 'an SCP also protects the management account'; 'Control Tower creates the organization trail' (no verified fact); 'member accounts cannot see the trail' (they can see it). Spoken numbers: none needed.

speak.prompt: Do we need AWS Control Tower, or is AWS Organizations enough?
speak.note: First sentence may start 'Both': both organize many accounts; the difference is that Control Tower builds and governs the accounts on top of Organizations. How it works: Organizations is the framework (accounts, OUs, policies, one bill); Control Tower adds a landing zone, Account Factory and controls. Watch: Control Tower has no charge of its own, but you pay for the services it turns on, such as AWS Config, and short-lived resources raise the AWS Config cost. In your case: 'How many accounts will you have next year, and who will build each new one?' Must not say: 'Control Tower replaces Organizations'; 'Control Tower costs nothing to run'.

diagrams.title: An SCP on an OU in an organization
diagrams.claim: An SCP on an organizational unit limits every member account below it, but not the management account.
diagrams.alt: An organization tree. The root holds the management account and two OUs, Security and Workloads. An SCP is attached to the Workloads OU and reaches its dev and prod accounts only.
say: Organizational units (OUs) group the member accounts under the root of the organization.
An SCP attached to the Workloads OU applies to every account in that OU.
A request in the prod account succeeds only if the SCPs and the IAM policies allow it.
SCPs do not restrict users or roles in the management account.
diagrams.note: Generic accounts, not Callvale's (the story stays in the Startup example and the Decision record). Groups form a tree: Organization > Root > Security OU (log archive account, audit account) and Workloads OU (dev account, prod account); the management account sits in the root group. At most 12 nodes. Steps 3 and 4 are strict text: link them in the Markdown (step 3 with iam-scp-faq-effective-permissions-intersection, step 4 with organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account). Step 3 uses 'only if' and so needs its link. No AWS number in labels.
